summary: Defines MIB objects for receiving notifications, called traps, from devices that support APPN and its DLUR capabilities. It lets an APPN network report events to management software. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: These are alarm bells that an older IBM style network device can ring to tell a manager something has happened.

questions: what is the appn traps mib
what notifications does the appn trap mib define
subtitle: SNMP notifications that let APPN and DLUR devices announce status changes instead of waiting to be polled.

tldr.problem: The APPN MIB lets a management station poll topology tables, but it has no way to poll the local topology tables (TGs, ports, link stations) for status changes, and the final accounting counts of an ending session are lost when its row is deleted.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB module defines six notifications (traps) for APPN and DLUR devices, plus an appnTrapControl object to switch them on and off and counters that let a manager notice a missed notification.
tldr.outcome: Managers get asynchronous status news and can poll less often. The module is a Proposed Standard from November 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 2456 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1998. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the APPN MIB in RFC 2455 and the DLUR MIB in RFC 2232.

sections.title: What the Module Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2456 is a product of the SNA NAU Services MIB Working Group. It defines a MIB module of notifications for devices with APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking) and DLUR (Dependent LU Requester) capabilities.

The module is written in SMIv2. The RFC uses the key words from RFC 2119, and it explains how the module fits the SNMP Management Framework: an architecture, a way to describe objects (the SMI), message protocols, protocol operations and fundamental applications.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of alarms that certain old-style network machines can sound when something changes, so a manager does not have to keep asking.

sections.title: The Polling Gap It Fills
sections.content:
The SNANAU APPN MIB (RFC 2455) and the SNANAU DLUR MIB (RFC 2232) let a management station read configuration and status. The APPN MIB can efficiently poll the network topology using flow reduction sequence numbers (FRSNs) as a table index. It has no such mechanism for the local topology tables: appnLocalTgTable, appnPortTable and appnLsTable.

This module closes that gap by letting the device send a notification when a row in one of these tables changes status. It also covers a second problem. Intermediate session statistics are collected mainly for accounting, but when a session ends its row is deleted from appnIsInTable, and everything counted since the last poll is lost. A notification can deliver those final numbers. If it is not delivered, they are lost, and the RFC suggests polling more often if that matters.

Many objects in the notifications are imported from the APPN and DLUR MIBs. Implementors of this MIB must also implement the APPN MIB. Implementations of the DLUR groups must also implement the DLUR MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, the manager had to keep knocking on the door to ask if anything changed. Now the machine can ring the doorbell itself, and it also sends a last report when a job finishes.

sections.title: The Six Notifications
sections.content:
The module groups its notifications under appnTrapMIB. Each one carries a change counter and the new state.

  • appnIsrAccountingDataTrap is sent when an intermediate session (ISR session) through the node is taken down, normally or not. It carries the final PIU and byte counts and the session up time.
  • appnLocalTgOperStateChangeTrap reports a change to appnLocalTgOperational in the local TG table.
  • appnLocalTgCpCpChangeTrap reports a change to appnLocalTgCpCpSession, the control-point to control-point (CP-CP) session state of a TG.
  • appnPortOperStateChangeTrap reports a port operational state change.
  • appnLsOperStateChangeTrap reports a link station operational state change.
  • dlurDlusStateChangeTrap reports a change of a DLUR-DLUS session status in dlurDlusTable.

The accounting counts in the first notification are not complete totals for the session, because they may have wrapped while it was up. The notification is not a substitute for polling.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six different bells: one for a finished job report, and one each for a road between machines, a doorway, a connection, a helper link and a helper session changing.

sections.title: When a Notification Is Sent
sections.content:
The rules avoid noise. Port and link operational states have intermediate states, but a notification is sent only when the state moves to active or inactive.

  • Row creation: a notification is sent only if the new row is already active or operational. This avoids one notification for an inactive new row and another when it is activated.
  • Row deletion: a notification is sent only if the last state was active or operational. In that case the notification reports the inactive state, since a deleted resource cannot be active.
  • CP-CP changes: appnLocalTgCpCpChangeTrap is sent when appnLocalTgCpCpSession changes but appnLocalTgOperational does not. It is never sent for row creation or deletion.

These notifications are more than a "poll me now" signal, because they carry the current state itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The machine only rings the bell for real news: when something turns on or off, not for every small step in between.

sections.title: Control and Change Counters
sections.content:
The supporting object appnTrapControl is a read-write BITS object with one bit for each of five notification types (bits 0 to 4). Setting a bit to 1 enables that type, subject to further filtering by the snmpNotificationMIB; setting it to 0 disables it. It exists so that implementations need not implement RFC 2273 just to control these notifications. The destination of the notifications is outside the scope of the module.

The accounting notification is the exception. It is controlled by the APPN MIB's appnIsInGlobeCtrAdminStatus: if intermediate session counts are kept at all, the notification is enabled.

Four Counter32 objects count status changes of rows since the APPN node was last reinitialized: appnLocalTgTableChanges, appnPortTableChanges, appnLsTableChanges and dlurDlusTableChanges. They increment whenever a condition arises that would cause a notification, whether or not it is enabled. If a manager sees the counts jump, it has missed a notification and should retrieve the whole table again.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an on/off switch for each bell, and a tally counter that goes up with every change. If the manager sees the tally skip a number, it knows it missed a bell and checks everything.

sections.title: Compliance and Groups
sections.content:
The compliance statement appnTrapMibCompliance makes groups conditionally mandatory. The ISR notification group is for nodes that report final ISR counter values. The topology configuration and notification groups are for nodes that support polling reduction for local topology, and the two DLUR groups are for nodes that support polling reduction for dlurDlusTable.

A node that implements a configuration group SHALL also implement the matching notification group, and the reverse. An agent is not required to support a set on appnTrapControl, so read-only access is allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: A machine picks the bells it wants to offer, but if it offers a switch for a bell it must also offer the bell.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some management information may be sensitive, so authentication of SNMP requests and controlled access SHOULD be used in such environments. The RFC points to the user-based security model for authentication and the view-based access control model for access control.

None of the read-only objects reports a password, user data or anything particularly sensitive. Some enterprises still treat network configuration, usage and performance as corporate assets and may restrict access. The one read-write object is appnTrapControl, which controls whether the notifications are generated.
sections.plainLanguage: The alarm list is not secret like a password, but a company may not want strangers listening, so it can lock the door.

items.desc: Final accounting counts when an ISR session is taken down.

items.label: appnLocalTgCpCpChangeTrap
items.desc: Local TG CP-CP session state changed.

items.label: appnLsOperStateChangeTrap
items.desc: Link station became active or inactive.

items.label: dlurDlusStateChangeTrap
items.desc: DLUR-DLUS session became active or inactive.
